speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: So, I know how much Members will be looking forward eagerly to this Bill with keen interest and the Ministry of Law will endeavour not to disappoint.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Globalisation has led to unprecedented growth in international trade and investment.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This has seen a corresponding increase in cross-border disputes, and a heightened demand for cross-border dispute resolution services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Current economic conditions notwithstanding, in the long term, international trade and, consequently, the need for international dispute resolution, are expected to grow.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The establishment of the ASEAN Economic Community in 2015, which allows for freer movement of goods, services, investments, skilled labour and capital in the region, will add to this demand.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Singapore is well-placed to meet this increased demand.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Today, we already offer a full suite of international dispute resolution services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In arbitration, we are one of the most preferred seats of arbitration in the world.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: For litigation, we recently established the Singapore International Commercial Court (SICC) to meet demand for commercial dispute resolution in the region and internationally.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: And for mediation, we established the Singapore International Mediation Centre to provide mediation services for international disputes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In the recently concluded Committee of Supply debates, the Minister for Law informed Members that the Government will create new frameworks to help our lawyers seize opportunities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Greater enforceability will make our Courts a more attractive forum for determining cross-border disputes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This, in turn, will generate more opportunities for our legal industry.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The implementation of the Convention also demonstrates Singapore's commitment to be a global player in facilitating international commerce.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Drawing more complex cross-border 	Page: 64 commercial cases to our Courts will allow us to develop and shape commercial law, as well as international jurisprudence, relating to the Convention.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Parties to commercial contracts commonly specify where disputes arising under the contract are to be resolved.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: If the parties specify that disputes arising from the contract are to be resolved in one jurisdiction to the exclusion of other jurisdictions, that is known as an exclusive choice of court agreement.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: If they specify one jurisdiction, but do not exclude other jurisdictions, then that is known as a non-exclusive choice of court agreement.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: When choosing the jurisdiction or forum to resolve their disputes, parties typically consider several factors, including whether the forum: (a) provides certainty as to how the law is to be interpreted and applied; (b) is a trusted forum, that is, neutral and not corrupt; (c) is competent and efficient in resolving disputes; and whether the judgment or award obtained can be easily enforced domestically and overseas.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This is particularly relevant where parties' assets are located in another jurisdiction.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Arbitral awards have wide enforceability because of the New York Convention.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In contrast, court judgments are generally more difficult to enforce in other jurisdictions, especially if the two jurisdictions concerned do not have reciprocal arrangements or treaties on the enforcement of judgments.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In common law jurisdictions, for example, a party would, generally, have to commence fresh proceedings in that other jurisdiction and sue on the court judgment as a debt.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: It can also be open to more challenges, especially if the defendant disputes that the original court had jurisdiction to make the judgment sought to be enforced.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The Convention provides greater certainty on where disputes between parties will be litigated and where judgments can be enforced.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: First, it establishes an international legal regime for upholding exclusive choice of court agreements in international civil or commercial cases.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Second, it governs the recognition and enforcement of judgments amongst courts of the contracting states.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In this regard, it does for court judgments of contracting states what the New York Convention does for arbitral awards.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Under the convention regime, parties will have greater assurance that: the court chosen by them under an exclusive choice of court agreement will hear their dispute and not some other 	Page: 65 courts; and the courts of contracting states will enforce the judgment of the chosen court.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This gives greater certainty which will, in turn, enable parties to better manage the risks involved in cross-border business and promote a more conducive legal environment for international trade investment.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: It is an opportune time for Singapore to implement and ratify the Convention.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Doing so will be beneficial to our position as a dispute resolution hub.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This includes judgments from SICC, which was established as a specialist court to hear international commercial disputes, including disputes which have no substantial connection to Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Second, the ability to enforce our judgments more widely will be an added incentive for parties to choose Singapore courts, including SICC, in exclusive choice of court agreements.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We have consulted various stakeholders, such as the Law Society, foreign law firms, academics and the Judiciary.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: They support the signing of the Convention as they recognise the benefit that will result from judgments of the Singapore Courts being more easily enforced or recognised in foreign jurisdictions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: I will now highlight some important features of the Bill.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: It does not apply to exclusive choice of court agreements in personal, family or consumer matters.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: It would not, therefore, apply to matrimonial matters, bankruptcy, insolvency, employment or personal injury.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Part 2 of the Bill deals with the jurisdiction of the Singapore Courts in cases of an exclusive choice of court agreement that falls within the scope of the Bill.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Briefly, if a Singapore Court is the chosen Court under an exclusive choice of court agreement, the Singapore Court will have the jurisdiction to decide the dispute at hand.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The Singapore Court, generally, cannot decline jurisdiction on the ground that the dispute should be decided by a court of another state.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Conversely, if the Singapore Court is not the chosen court, the Singapore Court must, generally, stay or dismiss the matter.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This addresses a situation where an action which is commenced in the High Court pursuant to an exclusive choice of court agreement specifying the Singapore High Court as the forum is subsequently transferred to SICC.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Clause 2(2) makes it clear that the High Court includes SICC and removes any doubt that the intention of this Bill is for the Convention regime to apply to SICC, notwithstanding the transfer.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Part 3 of the Bill relates to the recognition and enforcement of foreign judgments.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: However, the Convention provides certain limited 	Page: 66 grounds on which the Singapore Courts must or may refuse to recognise or enforce such foreign judgments.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Examples of where a foreign judgment will not be recognised or enforced include where the foreign judgment was obtained by fraud or where recognition and enforcement of the judgment would be against Singapore's public policy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In such instances, the Bill makes it mandatory for the Singapore Courts to refuse recognition and enforcement.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The Bill also provides certain discretionary grounds for refusal.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Declarations can be made under the Convention to exclude or modify its application to specific matters; to allow the Courts to refuse to hear disputes or decline to recognise and enforce foreign judgments in certain limited circumstances; or to extend the Convention obligations to non-exclusive choice of court agreements.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Singapore is currently not making any declarations, but the Bill provides the Minister with the power to make regulations to incorporate the effect of any such future declarations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The Bill only applies vis-à-vis other contracting states to the Convention.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: It would not apply where the court chosen under the exclusive choice of court agreement is a court of a non-contracting state.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I rise in support of the Choice of Court Agreements Bill.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For the rest of my speech, I shall refer this as the Convention of Hague or the Hague Convention.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Singapore joined the European Union (EU), the United States (US) and Mexico as the current states who have signed up to the Convention.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The present Bill is being passed to ratify the Convention and bring it into law in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Choice of court agreements are clauses in commercial contracts where parties to a contract nominate the courts of a particular country to decide on any legal disputes that may arise from the contract.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Convention seeks to provide uniformity in the way the courts of contracting states should decide on choice of court agreements in contracts.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In particular, it provides specific rules in the way the courts of contracting states can decide on how they should rule on exclusive choice of court 	Page: 67 agreements.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Convention also seeks to provide uniformity in the way the courts of contracting states will decide on the recognition and enforcement of foreign civil judgment of fellow contracting states.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Likewise, by way of reciprocity, our civil judgments may be recognised and enforced in the same 11 countries.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Our civil judgments may be recognised and enforceable in these additional countries and, likewise, we may recognise and enforce their courts' judgments.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Hopefully, the US will ratify the Convention soon.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: More than that, I hope that it will be a matter of time before other parties sign up to the Convention.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: When more countries sign up and ratify the Convention, more countries will be added to the 39 states.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The mutual recognition and enforcement of judgments among contracting states will certainly help to promote international trade.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The cooperation of contracting states and the recognition and enforcement of judgments will, hopefully, help to enhance our Courts as one of the leading judiciaries in the area of commercial law.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It has been said that the Hague Convention seeks to create a regime for recognition and enforcement of court judgments comparable to the Convention on the Recognition and Enforcement of Foreign Arbitral Awards, commonly referred to as the New York Convention.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Hopefully, in time to come, the Hague Convention will be as successful as the New York Convention.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Over the years, Singapore has grown to be a leading forum for international arbitration in the world.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: SIAC has become one of the leading international arbitration centres.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In more recent years, the Singapore Chamber of Maritime Arbitration (SCMA) has become a leading maritime arbitration body.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government has been trying to develop Singapore as an international dispute resolution centre.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: International arbitration is one pillar of this thrust.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The other pillar is our Courts, particularly where it involves adjudication of disputes arising from international contracts.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: By enhancing the enforceability of our Court judgments abroad, I hope that they can enhance the attraction of SICC and, indeed, Singapore Courts generally, and persuade more international commercial parties to have their disputes decided in our Courts.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: To this end, I am in support of the ratification of the Hague Convention and of this Bill.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I hope SICC will develop to be a premier international commercial Court.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Court has already appointed distinguished and reputable judges from different countries to sit on its bench.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But we also need to think about the mechanics of getting our Courts to be chosen as the exclusive choice of court in the jurisdiction clause of the commercial agreements that international parties enter into.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Page: 68 We have to persuade people to put Singapore Courts or SICC into their contracts as a court of choice to adjudicate any dispute that may arise.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We need to approach multinational corporations and other international companies.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We can start by persuading our own Singapore companies to use our SICC or Singapore jurisdiction clauses.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We need to persuade them to fight for such clauses to be used, even in the face of their international business counterparts disagreeing.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Jurisdiction clause is frequently not an item of priority to consider when parties are negotiating a contract.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: They may be more excited about the price of the contract or the operational details of the contract.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Most people think that jurisdiction clauses are not something that should break a deal.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This may make the task of persuading a change of mindset a little bit more difficult.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We need to persuade lawyers who draft contracts for their clients; sometimes, we need to persuade lawyers to persuade their clients.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: From my experience, some clients are creatures of habits and may take time to be persuaded.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We should also try to persuade the many international lawyers based in Singapore or in Asia to promote Singapore, whether for SICC or for arbitration.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We should take a leaf from the experience of SIAC and, in recent years, SCMA, their marketing efforts, to persuade companies to use their respective house of arbitration clauses.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Over time, SIAC has grown in its reputation and stature.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: On the other hand, SCMA has come a long way in the last few years.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: SCMA has become a much better known name in the international maritime circle.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The SCMA arbitration clause is becoming more and more widely used in the world.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Its contract forms are recognised and used by shipping companies worldwide as industry standard templates.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Persuading BIMCO to have an SCMA arbitration clause was no mean feat for a relatively young maritime body like SCMA.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Efforts like this should inspire all stakeholders in their promotion drives for not just arbitration in Singapore, but also in the use of SICC or Singapore Courts as a chosen choice of court for dispute resolution.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: One of the strengths of Singapore as a legal hub is that it can and often does provide a neutral forum for non-Singapore parties.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, for international arbitration, Singapore is often a preferred neutral forum of choice for a dispute involving, say, two Asian parties, for example, Chinese and Indian parties or between, say, a European party and a Chinese party.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, our Court judgment is not recognised in Indonesia.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I know that many Indonesians prefer to have their commercial disputes determined by arbitration in Singapore and frequently SIAC, and, sometimes, even when their business counterparts in the same contract are also Indonesians.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We should persuade our ASEAN neighbours to follow our footsteps in signing up to the Hague Convention.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I should declare my interest as a lawyer who practises dispute resolution and deals with cases that would be considered international cases under this Bill.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This Bill is an important development in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Singapore started developing as a centre for international dispute resolution in the 1980s.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: We became a party to the New York Convention on Enforcement of Arbitral Awards in 1986 and this heralded the rise of Singapore as a dispute resolution centre for international arbitration in the 1990s.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The importance of arbitration, and especially international arbitration, was manifold.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: First of all, it provided parties the opportunity to have their disputes resolved before a confidential forum.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It was a one-stop solution; there was no appeal on the arbitral award generally.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: But perhaps, most importantly for international disputes, it also allowed an arbitral award obtained in Singapore to be enforced in many other countries and, in particular, all the countries that are parties to the New York Convention.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: At the moment, there about 156 such countries.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: What this means is that parties who are involved in a dispute that involved multiple jurisdictions, can now choose any country that is a party to the New York Convention and that includes Singapore, have the dispute resolved there, and if that dispute is an international arbitration, they can enforce it in many other countries.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This has been an important attraction of international arbitration.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It is in this context that this Bill changes the equation somewhat.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: There are three key components to this Bill.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: But otherwise, if a court is chosen as the venue for dispute resolution, it has to take up the case.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This is even if the case has no other relationship with the country concerned.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, what this means is that even if the court might otherwise have had jurisdiction, as a result of this clause, they would have to decline to take up the case.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This is very similar to what happens in the arbitration framework as well.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: If a dispute is subject to arbitration and it is governed by the International Arbitration Act, typically the courts will stay any court cases that try to go around that clause.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This basically says that courts have to give effect to judgments from another contracting state.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: What these three mechanisms do is, in effect, they give judgments in Singapore an effect similar to an international arbitral award, in that a judgment that is made here can be enforced on any other party that is a contracting party to the Hague Convention.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It is in this respect that it is also important to look at some of the implications.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: There are still important differences between the two for parties that are 	Page: 70 deciding whether to choose to use arbitration or to use the Courts.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: As a practitioner, I can say that one the biggest advantages of the Courts is that where a dispute is complex and where non-parties may be involved, it is easier to get them involved if the dispute is in Court.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, it is one of the classic rules of arbitration that only parties to the arbitration agreement can bring their dispute in that arbitration agreement.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: If there is a dispute that involves the two parties in the arbitration agreement as well as non-parties, the only way the non-parties can get involved is with the consent of both parties to the arbitration agreement.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: However, if the same dispute is brought into Court, there is no such limitation on the Courts' power to bring the other parties involved in the dispute into that dispute, provided the Court otherwise has jurisdiction.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This actually gives the Courts a great deal more flexibility and, in fact, the choice of using a Court would give you more flexibility if you envision that your dispute may involve other parties.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, this is an important advantage the Courts have over arbitration.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This used to be counter-balanced by the limitation on enforceability of a Court award in other jurisdictions, but this Bill will remove that limitation somewhat.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It is also here that we come into one of the limitations of this new development and, that is, the number of contracting states.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The New York Convention for Arbitral Awards has about 156 parties.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: That means an international arbitration award can be enforced in 156 different countries.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Mexico was the first country to ratify it.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The EU was the second and that took place only in about October last year.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The EU brought in the other 27 countries.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Singapore is the next country to ratify it.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The US has signed it but has not yet ratified it.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: One of my suggestions, in fact, if we were to make this Bill even more meaningful, would be to try and get more of our friends to sign up to the Convention.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: We could start with ASEAN because a lot of our business is in ASEAN, and other trading partners as well, potentially India, China.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This would help to give the Bill even more reach because the more parties that ratify the Convention, the more we will allow the dual enforceability of court judgments.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Courts, otherwise, have a big advantage over arbitration as a forum for dispute resolution.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I should also caveat that there are some complex disputes for which even this Bill will not provide easy answers.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I explained that multi-party disputes are one of the biggest limitations of arbitration.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: For example, if a dispute were to occur entirely, say, in a third country, but the parties of that dispute ask for it to be resolved in a Court in Singapore and there were non-parties involved, it does not automatically follow the Singapore Court's jurisdiction over the non-parties.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, it does not overcome all the limitations but I think it still gives more flexibility to involve non-parties to the arbitration agreement.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The final thing I should point out is that there are some concerns that there is no limitation on which countries can become parties to this Convention.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: While we will not name specific countries, there are some countries where people have more doubts about the judicial systems.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Page: 71 For example, for an award where we may suspect the legitimacy of that judicial system, does it mean that we will automatically have to enforce it?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This was the criticism that was made about international arbitration as well when it first took off because, ultimately, parties choose their arbitrator.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: There is no real quality control over that.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: But overall, I think this is an excellent development.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I think it gives parties a great deal more choice in resolving their disputes.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: My only suggestion is that we wear our hats on the international front and get more people to sign up to the Convention.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: There are just a couple of points to which I should reply.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: First, Mr Vikram Nair raised the question of whether there was a limitation because of the relatively smaller number of contracting states.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The answer to that is we certainly expect it to grow.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But even with the present signatories as well as states that have ratified, it is already very promising.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Having the EU, for example, as a contracting party immediately extends our reach to the EU, save, of course, for Denmark.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In addition to that, the US and Ukraine are signatories to the Convention and there is growing interest in the Convention in the region.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We, for our part, will certainly, as suggested by Mr Dennis Tan and Mr Vikram Nair encourage more ASEAN member states to become parties to the Convention.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I think Mr Vikram Nair also raised the issue of what would happen if we are obliged to recognise judgments from Convention states with less robust systems and whether that would necessarily have to take place.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Possibly so, but I think that this is mitigated by two things.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: One is the element of choice; and second is built-in safeguards in the Bill.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Convention applies where there is an exclusive choice of court agreement.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, once they choose the forum, it means that parties have made a choice of that court.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: You have to assume that when they make that choice, they took into account the relevant factors, including the robustness of the judicial system of which that chosen court is a part.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This really means that they have taken it into account and what the Bill does is it gives effect to that choice.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It means parties must think carefully when choosing an exclusive choice of court forum.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Logically though, I think that this would act as a natural filter because, by and large, parties act rationally.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, they are likely to take into account the factors that I mentioned earlier – neutrality, that the system is not corrupt.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: They will look at the robustness of the system in which that court resides, and they will make their choices accordingly.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, that would act as a sort of natural filter.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Page: 72 Secondly, the Convention and the Bill have their own safeguards.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: For example, the Convention permits the Singapore Court to refuse recognition or enforcement of foreign judgments on certain specified grounds.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: There are also some discretionary grounds where the Courts can refuse recognition or enforcement.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Essentially, at the end of the day, what being a party to the Convention means is that it extends the enforceability of the judgments of our Courts and that, in turn, is good for the industry and for Singapore as a dispute resolution hub as a whole.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I am aware the Hague Convention has likewise in pari materia.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: However, may I know, just to understand the rationale behind it, as well the reasons?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Increasingly, we see employees being subjected to multi-jurisdictional kinds of arrangements.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It is in the realm of international trade and international investment and it is meant to address commercial disputes.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Employment matters fall under the category of more personal law where individuals are concerned.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: By their nature, they tend to be governed by more domestic regimes, and so it does not fall within the ambit of the Convention and, thus, does not come within this Bill.      .
